passages.happening:
God speaks directly to Aaron. “You and your sons and your father’s house must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary” (verse 1). The Levites are to join the priests and help them, but they must not come near the holy furniture or the altar (verses 2-3).

The purpose is stated. “And you shall attend to the duties of the sanctuary and of the altar, so that wrath may not fall on the Israelites again” (verse 5).

God calls both groups a gift. The Levites are ‘a gift to you’ (verse 6). And of the priests' own work he says, ‘I am giving you the work of the priesthood as a gift’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 17 ended with the people crying out that anyone who came near the tabernacle would die. This chapter is God's answer.

He does not answer by moving away. After Korah's revolt and the plague, God's presence stays in the middle of the camp. What he does is set a guard around it. The priests and Levites will stand between the holy place and the people, and they will carry the risk. The people will be able to live near God and not be destroyed.

The phrase ‘attend to the duties’ translates a Hebrew word that often means guard duty. Priests and Levites are sentries. They protect the people as much as they protect the sanctuary.

To ‘bear the iniquity’ of the sanctuary means to carry the responsibility for it. If the holy place is wrongly approached, the priests answer for it. The office Korah wanted as an honor is described here as a weight.

It is rare in the five books of Moses for God to speak to Aaron directly, without Moses. He does so three times in this chapter. After a revolt aimed at Aaron, God addresses him by name and confirms him.

And twice God uses the word ‘gift’. Korah had treated the priesthood as a prize to be seized. The chapter says it can only be received.
passages.later:
Peter gives the whole church a priestly name: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). What Korah grasped at wrongly is given, in Christ, to all God's people.

Hebrews answers the fear of coming near: ‘we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus’ (Hebrews 10:19).
passages.asks: God called the priests' hard and dangerous work a gift. Ask what responsibility you carry that you have thought of only as a weight. And ask whether you could receive it as something given to you for the sake of others.

passages.happening:
God tells Aaron what will belong to him and his sons. They receive a share of the most holy offerings: the grain offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings (verse 9). They receive the wave offerings, which their whole households may eat (verse 11).

“I give you all the freshest olive oil and all the finest new wine and grain that the Israelites give to the LORD as their firstfruits” (verse 12).

The firstborn of every womb belongs to them. But a firstborn son must be bought back, at five shekels of silver (verses 15-16). Firstborn cattle, sheep and goats are sacrificed, and the meat goes to the priests (verses 17-18).

“It is a permanent covenant of salt before the LORD for you and your offspring” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Priests had no farms. They could not serve at the altar and also work the land. So the law gives them a living from the gifts the people brought to God.

Israel lived by farming, and the gifts are counted in grain, wine, oil and animals. The firstfruits were the first and best of each harvest. Bringing them said that the whole harvest was God's. The firstborn of people and animals were his too, because he had spared Israel's firstborn on the night he struck Egypt (Exodus 13). A firstborn son was never sacrificed. He was bought back with silver, as chapter 3 explained. Five shekels was a real sum that a family could manage.

There is an order of holiness in the food. The most holy portions were eaten only by the priests themselves. The other gifts could be eaten by their wives, daughters and households, so long as they were ritually clean. The priest's whole family lived at God's table.

A ‘covenant of salt’ is a picture of something that lasts. Salt preserves, and it does not decay. The same phrase is used for God's promise of the kingship to David's family (2 Chronicles 13:5).

One more thing is worth seeing. What the people gave to God, God gave to the priests. An Israelite who brought his firstfruits was not paying a wage to a priest. He was giving to God, and God was feeding his servants.
passages.later:
Paul uses this arrangement when he writes about those who preach: “Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat of its food, and those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings? In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

The prophet Malachi later rebuked priests who offered blind and lame animals in place of the best (Malachi 1:8).
passages.asks: The people were to bring the first and best, not what was left over. Ask what God gets from you: the first of your time, money and strength, or what remains when everything else is paid for. And ask who serves you in the things of God, and whether they are cared for.

passages.happening:
God says to Aaron, “You will have no inheritance in their land, nor will you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (verse 20).

The Levites likewise receive no land. “Behold, I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do” (verse 21).

Then God gives Moses a word for the Levites themselves. From the tithe they receive, they must give a tenth to the LORD, ‘a tithe of the tithe’, and it goes to Aaron the priest (verses 26-28). It must be ‘from all the best of every gift’ (verse 29). The rest they and their households may eat anywhere, as their pay (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Verse 20 is the center of the chapter. When Israel reached Canaan, every tribe would be given a territory, to be passed down from parents to children. The Hebrew word is nachalah, an inheritance. In a farming world, land was security and a family's future.

The tribe of Levi was to have none. God gives the word a new meaning for them. He himself is their inheritance. The other tribes would point to their fields. The priests and Levites could point only to God.

That was a promise, and it was also a risk. The Levites' living depended on the faithfulness of the other tribes. When Israel was careless with its tithes, the Levites went hungry. The book of Nehemiah records a time when exactly that happened.

A tithe is a tenth. Israel's tenth went to the Levites as wages for their work at the tent. Deuteronomy describes other uses of the tithe, among them a feast and food for the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow (Deuteronomy 14). How these laws fit together was worked out in detail by later Jewish teachers.

The last part of the chapter closes a gap. The Levites lived on gifts. One might think that people who live on gifts are excused from giving. They are not. They too give a tenth, and it must be the best part. Everyone in Israel, including those who served at the tent, was a giver.

Later books show the arrangement in practice. Joshua 21 gives the Levites towns with pasture scattered among the tribes.
passages.later:
Believers who were not priests took up Aaron's promise as their own: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5). And another psalm says, “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).

Nehemiah found the system broken: “I also learned that because the portions for the Levites had not been given to them, all the Levites and singers responsible for performing the service had gone back to their own fields” (Nehemiah 13:10).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter mean that Christians must give a tenth?

Christians answer in more than one way.

Some hold that the tithe is a lasting standard. They note that Abraham gave a tenth before the law of Moses (Genesis 14:20), that Jesus speaks of tithing without setting it aside (Matthew 23:23), and that Paul applies the support of those who served at the altar to ministers of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

Others hold that the tithe belonged to the law of Moses and was tied to the Levites, the land and the temple, all of which are fulfilled in Christ. They note that the New Testament never commands a tenth. It calls for giving that is generous, glad and in keeping with what a person has (2 Corinthians 8 and 9). Many who hold this view still treat a tenth as a wise place to begin.

These notes take no side. The chapter's own concerns are clear on either view. God's people are to support those who serve in his worship. They are to give the best and not the leftovers. And even those who live on gifts are to give.

On one thing there is no room for doubt. No one may use this chapter to press money out of people who cannot afford it, or to promise that God will pay them back. If you gave money because you were pressed or frightened, or because someone promised that God would pay you back, and the return never came, that was not your failure. You were not lacking in faith. The promise was wrong. It may help to talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If you are in money trouble now, look for a trusted adviser where you live; these notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The Levites had no land to fall back on. God said that he was their portion. Ask what you count as your real security: your house, your savings, your work. And ask what it would mean to say of God, as the psalm does, that he is your portion.
